analysis.one_liner: Funds the IRS to audit more high earners and large corporations and raises penalties on the richest filers.
analysis.headline: The Stop CHEATERS Act was introduced in May 2021 with three cosponsors and never received a committee vote or any floor action before the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would send tens of billions in new funding to the IRS through 2031, mostly for enforcement aimed at people making over $1 million and corporations with over $20 billion in assets. It sets audit targets, raises the penalty for underpaying taxes to 40% for people making over $5 million, requires banks to report yearly totals of deposits and withdrawals on accounts, and adds money for taxpayer services and updated IRS technology. It died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever coming up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers who pay what they owe, since stronger enforcement of high earners and large corporations narrows the gap between taxes owed and taxes paid and relieves pressure to make up the difference elsewhere. Taxpayers who deal with the IRS would also get better service and faster help, since the bill funds pre-filing assistance, advocacy services, and a technology overhaul.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Honest taxpayers who pay their share

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates $1.6 billion in 2022 rising to $6.8 billion a year through 2031 for IRS enforcement, plus $2 billion a year for taxpayer services and $800 million a year for operations support and technology modernization.

Sets audit goals starting in 2025: 50% of individual returns reporting income of $10 million or more, 95% of corporation returns for companies with more than $20 billion in assets, and 40% of estate tax returns for estates above $10 million.
Raises the accuracy-related underpayment penalty to 40% of the underpayment for taxpayers with taxable income above $5 million, up from the standard 20%.

States a goal of reducing the tax gap, the share of taxes due that go unreported and unpaid, by at least one-third within ten years, and directs the IRS to report to Congress every two years on shifting enforcement toward high-income filers and on revenue lost to offshore evasion.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and large corporations, who would face sharply higher audit odds and, for the largest underpayments, penalties up to 40%. Banks and financial institutions would bear the cost of a new annual reporting requirement covering every account they maintain. The spending itself would be federal appropriations.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, big corporations, and banks

drawbacks.text: The bank reporting provision covers every account, not just those of the wealthy: covered financial institutions would have to report the total deposits and withdrawals on each account they maintain each year, which raised privacy concerns and compliance costs for banks and their customers.

Expanded audits can reach beyond billionaires: the bill sets an audit goal for 0.22% of employment tax returns, which are filed by employers of all sizes, so some ordinary businesses would face closer IRS scrutiny.

The bill is expensive, committing roughly $65 billion over a decade in new appropriations, and the revenue it recovers depends on how effectively the IRS can hire and retain auditors capable of untangling complex high-income returns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core case is strong on its own terms: IRS enforcement of high-income and corporate returns has historically returned more in collected taxes than it costs, and the bill pairs enforcement with money for better taxpayer service. The weakest part is the blanket bank reporting requirement, which sweeps in every American account holder rather than targeting the high-income evasion it is meant to catch; a version that narrowed the reporting would have blunted the strongest objection.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced with three cosponsors in May 2021, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never brought up again before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Angus King, an independent from Maine, introduced the bill on May 26, 2021, joined by Senators Sherrod Brown and Tim Kaine.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced.
Its only cosponsors were three Democrats, and no Republican signed on.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never marked it up, and it never received a vote in the Senate or the House before the 117th Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners, large corporations, and banks are better off because the bill died: none of the new audit targets, 40% penalties, or account reporting requirements ever took effect.

for.name: Sen. Angus King
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to fund IRS enforcement of high earners and large corporations.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Banking industry trade associations
against.role: Banks and financial institutions facing a new account reporting requirement
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to require financial institutions to report annual account inflows and outflows to the IRS, raising privacy objections during the same 2021 debate this bill's reporting provision came from.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, but the bill's sponsors and all three cosponsors were a Senate independent and three Democrats, with no Republican support, in a chamber split 50 Republicans to 48 Democrats and 2 independents.

industries.note: The bill sets audit goals reaching 50% of returns with income of $10 million or more and raises the underpayment penalty to 40% for income above $5 million. Their gain in avoiding these costs would come at the expense of the tax revenue other taxpayers effectively make up.

industries.industry: Large corporations (more than $20 billion in assets)
industries.note: The bill sets a goal of auditing 95% of returns from the largest corporations each year. Larger audit capacity means more unpaid tax identified and paid.

New section 6050Z would require every covered financial service provider to file an annual return reporting total deposits and withdrawals for each account it maintains. The compliance cost falls on banks while the enforcement benefit flows to the public.
The bill sets a goal of auditing 40% of estate tax returns for estates valued above $10 million, increasing scrutiny of large inherited-wealth transfers.
